interest: This file offers valuable historical insight into Axis intelligence re-alignments in neutral Europe during the final phase of World War II, specifically the late-1944 shift of Japanese clandestine networks from the Iberian Peninsula to Scandinavia. The OSS intelligence roster provides granular prosopographical and operational details on prominent intelligence figures like Major General Makoto Onodera and his subordinates, illuminating how Japanese diplomatic and press agencies (particularly Domei, Asahi, and Yomiuri-Hochi) functioned as covers for covert intelligence gathering and liaison with German services. Furthermore, the internal State Department memoranda between Far Eastern Affairs and naval security officers expose contemporary administrative friction regarding wartime 'Top Secret' overclassification and the protection of intelligence sources, while the diplomatic traffic highlights the quiet cooperation between Allied legations and Swedish authorities in monitoring Axis operatives on neutral territory.
overview: This State Department decimal file (894.20258) documents United States diplomatic and intelligence surveillance of Japanese military, espionage, and propaganda operations in neutral Sweden during late 1944. Triggered by reports that Japan was shifting its primary European intelligence hub from Lisbon to Stockholm following Allied advances in Western Europe, the correspondence tracks the movements of Japanese diplomats, military and naval attachés, diplomatic couriers, and accredited journalists traveling between Berlin, Helsinki, and Stockholm. Centered on communications from American Minister Herschel V. Johnson and the Department of State, the file incorporates a comprehensive Office of Strategic Services (OSS) roster identifying suspected intelligence operatives in Sweden, internal departmental debates over the proper security classification of intelligence despatches, and confirmations that Swedish authorities were actively monitoring Japanese press correspondents for espionage activities.

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Hull instructs the Stockholm Legation to investigate reports that the Japanese are transferring their European intelligence center from Lisbon to Sweden.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull cables the American Legation in Stockholm regarding confidential reports that the Japanese are moving their European intelligence operations from Lisbon to Stockholm. The Legation is instructed to telegraph any evidence of such an operational relocation and to keep Washington closely informed of all future developments. The telegram is sent top secret under strict distribution controls.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1733 from Secretary of State Hull to American Legation, Stockholm

subfiles.about: The State Department informs the Stockholm Legation of intelligence from Madrid regarding Japanese attachés departing Lisbon and Barcelona for Sweden.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State relays intelligence received from the U.S. Embassy in Madrid concerning Japanese personnel movements toward Sweden. It reports that Attaché Tohan Dando of the Japanese Embassy in Lisbon departed Barcelona on September 8 destined for Sweden, and identifies Attachés Ono and Nemoto as other likely transfers. The message references Stockholm's prior telegram No. 3568 regarding the rumored intelligence shift.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1837 from Department of State to American Legation, Stockholm

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson reports that the Legation cannot yet confirm the intelligence transfer from Lisbon but is preparing a roster of Japanese arrivals in Stockholm.
subfiles.summary: Minister Herschel V. Johnson informs the Secretary of State that the Legation cannot yet definitively determine whether Japan is relocating its intelligence center from Lisbon to Stockholm. He recommends comparing lists of known Japanese intelligence personnel in Lisbon against a comprehensive list of Japanese travelers arriving and departing Stockholm since October 1943, which the Legation is forwarding by mail. Johnson confirms that the Legation's investigation into the matter is actively continuing.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3568 from Herschel V. Johnson to Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Administrative record sheet documenting the filing, indexing, and security reclassification of Despatch No. 4079.
subfiles.summary: This Department of State cross-reference sheet and file wrapper records the receipt, routing, and official filing of document 894.20258/9-1244 (Stockholm Despatch No. 4079). It documents the document's entry into the Department's Confidential File on November 17–18, 1944, and notes changes in classification authority. Administrative indexing stamps and filing notations track its movement through departmental communication channels.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference and File Sheet for Despatch No. 4079 (894.20258/9-1244)

subfiles.about: Commander Parke concurs with downgrading Despatch No. 4079 to protect intelligence sources without maintaining excessive Top Secret classifications.
subfiles.summary: Commander L. W. Parke responds to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding the security classification of Stockholm Despatch No. 4079. He concurs that the document should be downgraded to Confidential, or at most Secret, to adequately safeguard the source of the intelligence. Parke observes that educating Foreign Service personnel on appropriate classification practices is an ongoing process, and recommends formally modifying the document's status in accordance with administrative security instructions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Commander L. W. Parke to Erle R. Dickover regarding Classification of Despatch No. 4079

subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs recommends downgrading Despatch No. 4079 from Top Secret to Confidential to prevent the dilution of the Top Secret classification.
subfiles.summary: Erle R. Dickover of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs writes to security officer Commander Parke urging that Despatch No. 4079 from Stockholm be downgraded. He notes that minimizing the volume of Top Secret documents reduces the need for burdensome security facilities and preserves the integrity of the highest classification tier. Dickover argues that nothing in the Stockholm despatch warrants Top Secret handling, suggesting the Legation merely adopted the classification from the enclosed OSS report, and recommends downgrading it to Confidential.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Erle R. Dickover to Commander L. W. Parke regarding Classification of Despatch No. 4079

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson transmits an Office of Strategic Services report documenting Japanese air travel to and from Sweden since October 1943.
subfiles.summary: Minister Herschel V. Johnson submits Despatch No. 4079 to the Secretary of State, forwarding a detailed report compiled by the Office of Strategic Services in Stockholm concerning Japanese air travel since October 1943. The submission directly supplements earlier telegraphic exchanges regarding the suspected transfer of Japanese intelligence operations from Lisbon to Stockholm. Johnson highlights the OSS's qualification that first-time arrivals cannot be definitively distinguished from returning residents, but emphasizes that all listed Japanese individuals are suspected of engaging in intelligence activity.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4079 from Herschel V. Johnson to Secretary of State Transmitting OSS Report

subfiles.about: An Office of Strategic Services roster and analysis of Japanese diplomats, attachés, couriers, and journalists in Sweden suspected of intelligence work.
subfiles.summary: This four-page intelligence report, enclosed with Despatch No. 4079, details Japanese air movements to and from Sweden between October 1943 and September 1944. An introductory note explains that the list records air passengers only and notes that some entries represent established Stockholm residents returning from official journeys to Berlin or Helsinki. The ensuing roster profiles dozens of Japanese officials—including Military Attaché General Makoto Onodera, Naval Attaché Iori Mishina, intelligence directors Jiro Homma and Joichi Inouye, diplomatic couriers, and news correspondents—providing dates of birth, local residential addresses in Stockholm, and specific dates of travel across Axis-controlled Europe.
subfiles.title: OSS Report: 'Japanese in Sweden' (Enclosure to Despatch No. 4079)

subfiles.about: Minister Johnson reports on accredited Japanese journalists arriving in Stockholm from Berlin and notes Swedish surveillance of their activities.
subfiles.summary: Minister Herschel V. Johnson communicates an updated intelligence summary of Japanese press correspondents accredited to the Swedish Foreign Office who recently relocated to Stockholm from Berlin. The journalists listed represent major media outlets including Asahi Shimbun, Yomiuri-Hochi, Mainichi, and Domei, with recent autumn arrival dates specified for Okumura, Sasaki, and Enna. Johnson concludes by reporting that Swedish authorities have officially given assurances that these Japanese journalists will be kept under close surveillance for possible espionage activities.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 5294 from Herschel V. Johnson to Secretary of State on Japanese Journalists in Sweden
